name: Sparks from Amber: How Electricity Lit the World
description: Rubbed amber, kites in thunderstorms, rival currents and giant dams: the long road from a curious spark to the power grid that runs everything.

checkpoints.name: Amber and lightning
checkpoints.note: Thales is said to have noticed that rubbed amber attracts feathers. Two thousand years later Franklin showed that lightning is the same force as the sparks of the laboratory and invented the lightning rod.

checkpoints.name: Batteries, magnets and wires
checkpoints.note: Volta's pile of 1800 gave the first steady current, and Faraday found that magnets can make current, pointing to motors and generators. The telegraph and Morse's code sent signals along wires, a cable crossed the Atlantic, and Maxwell tied electricity and light together.

checkpoints.name: Lights and currents
checkpoints.note: Bell's telephone and Edison's lamp were followed by the first power stations. Edison backed direct current, Tesla and Westinghouse backed alternating current, and the war of the currents was decided by distance.

checkpoints.name: The grid
checkpoints.note: Big dams such as Hoover and steam turbines feeding long wires tied whole regions to electric power, Marconi's radio sent signals without wires, and the first solar cell in 1954 hinted at a different source.

checkpoints.name: New sources
checkpoints.note: Batteries made lithium-ion packs for phones and cars, wind and sunlight began to feed grids, and projects such as the Three Gorges Dam show electricity still shaping rivers and nations.
